candidateRows: The defensible mythicist thesis holds that Jesus acquired a mortal Jewish body but underwent death and resurrection in a heavenly mythic realm, paralleling ancient savior cults.
This passage defines Carrier's precise position and supplies the comparative-religion framework on which his celestial interpretation of Paul rests.
Carrier distinguishes his position from denying that Jesus had flesh, then compares Christianity with cults whose earthly narratives allegorized celestial salvific events.
Paul's authentic letters never unambiguously locate Jesus's life, death, burial, or resurrection on earth and can instead be read as describing a heavenly cosmic drama.
This directly advances the central textual case that the earliest Christian documents do not establish an earthly Jesus and remain compatible with celestial mythicism.
Carrier turns to the seven letters he accepts as authentic, emphasizes their silence about an earthly ministry, and argues that ancient heavenly settings make their location ambiguous.
Restricting the Pauline corpus to seven letters is unwarranted because the scholarly conclusions against Pauline authorship of all thirteen letters rest on disputed foundations.
The authorship dispute determines which Pauline statements may enter the debate and therefore materially affects the available historical evidence about Jesus.
Carrier's restriction of admissible Pauline evidence to seven letters regarded as authentic
McLatchie challenges Carrier's minimal Pauline corpus, invokes Carrier's own criticism of authorship consensus, and argues that all thirteen letters are plausibly Pauline.
The Pauline epistles contain numerous biographical claims placing Jesus within earthly Jewish history, including ancestry, birth, teachings, associates, betrayal, and execution.
The cumulative list directly contests the claim that Paul supplies no earthly biography and presents the affirmative textual basis for Pauline historicity.
Carrier's argument that Paul never places Jesus's career or salvific death within earthly history
McLatchie inventories Pauline references he understands as earthly biographical data, then selects the rulers who crucified Jesus as the first passage for detailed examination.

The rulers who crucified Jesus in First Corinthians are more plausibly demonic powers because their terminology, salvific ignorance, and relation to Romans 13 fit a cosmic conflict better than human authorities.
Identifying the crucifying rulers is a decisive test of whether Paul located Jesus's death among earthly authorities or within a celestial drama.
McLatchie's use of First Corinthians 2 as Pauline evidence that human rulers crucified Jesus
Carrier argues that the relevant expression can denote demons, compares a contemporary heavenly-crucifixion tradition, and claims human rulers' motives conflict with Paul's account elsewhere.
A celestial crucifixion would have been intelligible within ancient Jewish cosmology because heavenly realms were believed to contain copies of earthly places, objects, and practices.
This answers a major plausibility objection to the celestial thesis by explaining how an earthly execution form could occur within the proposed heavenly setting.
The objection that crucifixion is intrinsically an earthly execution and therefore implausible in a celestial realm
Carrier appeals to ancient beliefs that earthly realities had heavenly counterparts and argues that demonic agents could therefore enact a copied form of crucifixion above.
The literary context of First Corinthians consistently concerns human wisdom and human rulers, so the rulers who crucified Jesus should be understood as earthly rather than demonic authorities.
This is the principal historicist rebuttal on the disputed crucifixion passage and directly supports an earthly location for the death Paul describes.
Carrier's interpretation of the rulers in First Corinthians 2 as celestial demonic forces
McLatchie compares usage in Romans and surrounding Corinthian passages, traces the contrast between human and divine wisdom, and argues that the temporal language remains ordinary.
The vocabulary of First Corinthians alone leaves the rulers' identity indeterminate, while the contrast with Romans 13 modestly favors interpreting them as celestial forces.
This preserves Carrier's celestial reading after McLatchie's contextual challenge by reframing the wording as ambiguous and restoring the theological-consistency argument.
McLatchie's claim that the Corinthian context makes the rulers unmistakably human authorities
Carrier concedes that the contested terminology can refer to either class of ruler but argues that their thwarting motives conflict with Paul's treatment of God-appointed rulers.
The context of 1 Corinthians 2 concerns human rulers, while allowing that demonic forces may also have supported the crucifixion.
This directly contests the celestial reading of the rulers who crucified Jesus, a major Pauline passage bearing on the debate motion.
Carrier's claim that the rulers in 1 Corinthians 2 are more plausibly demonic powers than earthly authorities.
Carrier had argued that Paul's contrast with Romans 13 favors demonic rulers; McLatchie answers from the surrounding human context and distinguishes participation from identity.
Paul's phrase brother of the Lord can denote an ordinary baptized Christian, and Galatians does not clearly identify James as Jesus's biological sibling.
The status of James as Jesus's biological brother is direct Pauline evidence for or against an earthly historical Jesus.
The historicist contention that Paul's incidental reference to James as the Lord's brother necessarily identifies Jesus's biological sibling.

After the moderator raises James as apparently incidental evidence for a real sibling, Carrier argues that all baptized Christians were brothers of the Lord and explains James's mention through Paul's apostolic-status argument.
Paul likely means a biological brother because other early Christian texts identify Jesus's brothers, including James, alongside his mother.
This supplies a direct historicist interpretation of Paul's James reference and connects it to traditions about Jesus's earthly family.
Carrier's argument that brother of the Lord merely distinguishes a non-apostolic baptized Christian rather than a biological relative.
McLatchie acknowledges scholarly grammatical debate, then invokes 1 Corinthians 9, Matthew, and Acts, arguing that mention beside Jesus's mother supports biological kinship.
First Corinthians 9 remains ambiguous about biological brothers, while later Gospel family traditions cannot establish what Paul himself believed.
The move directly resists claimed Pauline evidence of Jesus's earthly family and challenges using later narratives to interpret Paul's language.
McLatchie's appeal to 1 Corinthians 9, Matthew, and Acts as mutually supporting evidence that James was Jesus's biological brother.
Carrier interprets Paul's contrast as apostolic versus non-apostolic Christians, calls the Pauline wording vague, and treats Gospel family accounts as later legends potentially constructed from Paul.
Acts is agenda-driven fictionalized history whose possible sources cannot be cleanly separated from its embellishments and alterations.
Acts' historical reliability determines whether its earthly Jesus narrative can corroborate Pauline historicity through a companion of Paul.

Asked to summarize his view, Carrier describes Luke as promoting Roman favor, Christian lawfulness, and church harmony through crafted stories, while allowing an uncertain skeleton of sourced history.
Undesigned correspondences between Paul's letters and Acts support Acts' substantial historical accuracy and Luke's status as Paul's traveling companion.
The argument underwrites using Acts and Luke as historically informed evidence connecting Paul with an earthly conception of Jesus.
Carrier's portrayal of Acts as largely fictional, agenda-driven history whose sourced facts cannot reliably be distinguished from invention.
McLatchie uses the timing of Timothy's journey in 1 Corinthians and Acts as a jigsaw-like correspondence that he argues was not deliberately manufactured.
Accurate incidental details or use of Pauline sources cannot validate Acts because Acts contradicts Paul's own chronology, mission, and account of the Torah-free gospel.
This directly attacks the evidential bridge from Acts' incidental accuracy to its reliability about Paul and an earthly historical Jesus.
McLatchie's undesigned-coincidence argument that converging incidental details in Acts and Paul's letters substantiate Acts' historical veracity.
Carrier argues that source use does not identify invention, then contrasts Acts with Paul on Judean visibility, Arabia, Gentile mission, Peter, chronology, and Theudas.
Acts can telescope Paul's Arabian interval, and cumulative undesigned coincidences plus external corroborations make wholesale literary dependence implausible.
The move defends Acts against claimed Pauline contradictions and reinforces its value as evidence from within Paul's historical network.
Carrier's claims that Acts erases Paul's Arabian mission, contradicts authentic letters, and merely repurposes sources while altering their history.
McLatchie reads many days as compatible with a three-year interval, distinguishes undesigned interlocking details from copying, and adds examples involving Ananias and Ephesian proconsuls.
Luke's use of authentic source material for incidental details does not establish the truth of the rest of Acts' narrative.
This states the governing rebuttal to McLatchie's corroboration case and limits what Acts can establish about Paul and Jesus.
McLatchie's contention that difficult incidental corroborations show Acts was written from eyewitness-quality historical knowledge rather than fiction.
Carrier grants that Luke used sources but denies that such use authenticates the remaining narrative, then turns to the alleged reconciliation of Acts with Paul's Arabian journey.
If Acts was written by Paul's traveling companion, its thoroughly historical Jesus is difficult to reconcile with the claim that Paul taught a celestial Jesus.
This explicitly connects the disputed authorship and reliability of Acts to the central choice between Paul's earthly and celestial Jesus conceptions.
After extended debate over Acts, McLatchie argues that a genuine Pauline companion would not plausibly produce Acts and Luke's historical Jesus if Paul's own Jesus were celestial.
Luke-Acts cannot be treated as near-Pauline testimony because Luke's companionship with Paul and the work's authorship cannot be established.
This challenges a principal route from Acts and Luke to early historical testimony about Jesus and therefore bears directly on the historicity case.
McLatchie's claim that Luke traveled with Paul and authored Luke-Acts as informed historical testimony.
After the host summarizes the competing historical and celestial accounts, Carrier contests the claimed Pauline proximity of Luke-Acts before discussion turns to its narrative voice.
The first-person plural passages, external corroboration, and undesigned coincidences jointly support Luke being Paul's traveling companion.
Establishing the author's proximity to Paul would materially strengthen the claim that Luke-Acts preserves historically informed early Christian testimony.
Carrier's denial that Luke can be established as Paul's traveling companion or the informed author of Luke-Acts.
In response to questions about the first-person narration in Acts, McLatchie argues cumulatively from internal narrative features and external corroboration.
The first-person plural sea-voyage passages are a known literary device and do not establish that Acts was written by a companion of Paul.
The argument undercuts a key internal-authorship inference used to connect Acts closely to Paul and to credit its historical presentation.
McLatchie's inference that the first-person plural passages help identify Luke as a genuine traveling companion of Paul.
Carrier answers the appeal to Acts' narrative voice by separating intended narration from truth and by identifying comparable fictional voyage conventions.
Interlocking incidental details across the Gospels are best explained as undesigned coincidences arising from genuine historical events.
This supplies McLatchie's principal positive Gospel-based reason for treating the narratives as historically grounded rather than later fabricated settings.
Asked what Gospel features resist a fabrication account, McLatchie develops two cross-narrative examples involving the feeding narrative and Passion-week chronology.
John's use and rewriting of earlier Gospels explains the apparent interlocking details as designed literary correspondences rather than independent historical corroboration.
Source dependence offers a direct alternative explanation for the principal Gospel evidence McLatchie advances against literary fabrication.
McLatchie's argument that dispersed interlocking Gospel details constitute undesigned historical coincidences.
Carrier responds to the two Gospel examples by treating John as a literary reworking of existing Gospel source material whose correspondences are intentional.
The feeding narrative's relevant details are too dispersed and incompletely stated for deliberate reconciliation by the author of John to be plausible.
The move defends the independence and evidential force of the feeding example against Carrier's source-dependence explanation.
Carrier's contention that John deliberately rewrote earlier Gospel materials and thereby created the apparent correspondence.
Following the host's clarification of the dispute, McLatchie emphasizes that the location and disciple details are scattered among different chapters and works.
An author adapting source material can select suitable characters without restating every background detail, so omission of the location does not imply independence.
This supplies the mechanism needed for Carrier's literary-dependence account to explain the precise feeding-narrative correspondence raised by McLatchie.
McLatchie's claim that scattered and omitted details make deliberate literary construction of the feeding correspondence unlikely.
Carrier argues that a rewriting author need not flag the relevant city and can simply choose characters already associated with the source setting.
A cumulative body of close Synoptic-Johannine correspondences is less plausibly dismissed as isolated coincidence or routine literary borrowing.
The cumulative formulation broadens the dispute beyond one example and states why the proposed evidence is intended to survive localized alternative explanations.
Carrier's source-use mechanism for explaining the apparent hand-in-glove fit between John and the Synoptic narratives.
McLatchie shifts from the individual feeding example to the claimed cumulative force of numerous close narrative correspondences across the Gospels.
The cumulative correspondences remain expected if John repeatedly based his versions of stories on the earlier narrative source material.
The interjection answers the cumulative-evidence formulation by extending the same literary mechanism across multiple narrative correspondences.
McLatchie's appeal to the cumulative number of Synoptic-Johannine correspondences rather than any single example.
During McLatchie's cumulative argument, Carrier interjects that repeated correspondences follow naturally from repeated use of the same source narratives.
John's narrative purpose did not require identifying the city, so the absence of that detail provides no evidence against literary dependence.
This directly rebuts the claimed expectation that a dependent author would identify the location and thereby closes the detailed Gospel-source dispute.
McLatchie's claim that deliberate reconciliation should have led John to state the relevant city or associated background detail.
At the end of the exchange, Carrier argues that later historians' desire for geographic specificity was irrelevant to John's storytelling goals.
